author: Herwig, Holger H.
title: The Marne, 1914: The Opening of World War I and the Battle That Changed the World
notes: The standard modern operational narrative of the 1914 campaign in the West; uses German, French and British archives. Primary source for army movements, dates and strengths.

author: Tuchman, Barbara W.
title: The Guns of August
notes: Narrative classic covering the July Crisis to the eve of the Marne. Vivid on personalities; operational detail is dated — cite Herwig or the official histories for numbers and positions.

author: Strachan, Hew
title: The First World War, Volume I: To Arms
notes: Global, thematic; strongest on war plans, mobilization and the strategic context.

author: Zuber, Terence
title: Inventing the Schlieffen Plan: German War Planning 1871–1914
notes: Revisionist: argues the 1905 memorandum was not an operational plan and that 'the Schlieffen Plan' was a post-war construction. Contested — see Mombauer, Holmes, Foley; cite as one side of the debate.

author: Mombauer, Annika
title: Helmuth von Moltke and the Origins of the First World War
notes: Moltke the Younger's planning and conduct in 1914; the principal reply to Zuber on the reality of the plan.

author: Keegan, John
title: The First World War
notes: General history; clear chapters on the war plans and the 1914 campaign.

author: Hastings, Max
title: Catastrophe: Europe Goes to War 1914
notes: 1914 from the July Crisis to the trench line; good on the human scale and the Belgian and Serbian fronts.

author: Reichsarchiv
title: Der Weltkrieg 1914 bis 1918. Die militärischen Operationen zu Lande, Band 1: Die Grenzschlachten im Westen
notes: German official history; volumes 1, 3 and 4 cover the West in 1914. Authoritative for German orders of battle, daily positions and orders; apologetic in tone on command decisions, and it measures the campaign by what the German army did — the Belgian and French sides appear only as resistance met. Band 1, pp. 105–120 ('Die Eroberung der Festung Lüttich') is the account of the Liège operation and the reduction of the twelve forts, and is this pack's citation for when each of them fell: it gives the day and the part of the day — an afternoon, a forenoon, an evening — and not the clock. Page references are to the 1925 first edition, digitised at the URL above. Where a fort-by-fort record at clock resolution is wanted, the works to bring in are Donnell and Zuber (docs/sources.md, 'To add as the content lands').

author: Edmonds, J. E.
title: Military Operations: France and Belgium, 1914, Volume I: Mons, the Retreat to the Seine, the Marne and the Aisne, August–October 1914
publisher: Macmillan, London (History of the Great War based on Official Documents)
notes: British official history. Authoritative for the BEF's daily positions and the Le Cateau/Marne/Aisne narrative. The volume was revised twice; where this pack gives a page number for Volume I it cites source:edmonds-1933, the third edition, because that is the edition that is digitised and was read. Page numbers do not carry between the two.

author: Ministère de la Guerre, État-major de l'Armée, Service historique
title: Les Armées françaises dans la Grande Guerre, Tome I, 1er volume: La guerre de mouvement (opérations antérieures au 14 novembre 1914)
notes: French official history with annex volumes of orders (e.g. Instruction générale no 2, the 6 September order of the day). Authoritative for French orders of battle and positions.

author: Wikipedia contributors
title: Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia (English)
notes: Used only for uncontested biographical dates (birth, death) pending the citation standard in sand-23b.1. Never cite for operational claims.

author: Pais, Abraham
title: 'Subtle is the Lord…': The Science and the Life of Albert Einstein
notes: The standard scientific biography; relativity 1907–1919, the Entwurf theory, the 1914 eclipse expedition, the counter-manifesto.

author: Crelinsten, Jeffrey
title: Einstein's Jury: The Race to Test Relativity
notes: The astronomers and the eclipse tests 1911–1922, incl. Freundlich's 1914 expedition and internment.

author: Heilbron, J. L.
title: H. G. J. Moseley: The Life and Letters of an English Physicist, 1887–1915
notes: Moseley's law, his enlistment in 1914 and death at Gallipoli.

author: Ungern-Sternberg, Jürgen von; Ungern-Sternberg, Wolfgang von
title: Der Aufruf 'An die Kulturwelt!': Das Manifest der 93 und die Anfänge der Kriegspropaganda im Ersten Weltkrieg
notes: Text, signatories, genesis and aftermath of the Manifesto of the 93.

author: Beesly, Patrick
title: Room 40: British Naval Intelligence 1914–1918
notes: The Admiralty's signals-intelligence section from the 1914 codebook captures to the Zimmermann telegram; the forward link from 1914 wireless.

author: Horne, John; Kramer, Alan
title: German Atrocities, 1914: A History of Denial
notes: The standard study of the August 1914 reprisals in Belgium and France and of the franc-tireur myth; for the Belgian chapter and the historiography notes.

author: Edmonds, J. E.
title: Military Operations: France and Belgium, 1914, Volume II: Antwerp, La Bassée, Armentières, Messines and Ypres, October–November 1914
publisher: Macmillan, London (History of the Great War based on Official Documents)
notes: British official history, second volume. Its opening chapters cover the Belgian field army's withdrawal into Antwerp, the sorties of August and September, and the siege; the daily positions used here.

author: Tyng, Sewell
title: The Campaign of the Marne 1914
notes: Operational narrative from the interwar official histories; clear on the detached corps — Antwerp, Namur, Maubeuge — and on the Belgian 4th Division's journey round by Le Havre and Ostend.

author: Steg, Jean-Michel
title: Le jour le plus meurtrier de l'histoire de France: 22 août 1914
notes: The reconstruction, from the French Army's own death records, of the roughly 27,000 French soldiers killed on 22 August 1914; the source for the figure and for Rossignol and the Ardennes that day.

author: Spears, Edward L.
title: Liaison 1914: A Narrative of the Great Retreat
notes: Memoir of the British liaison officer at Lanrezac's 5th Army headquarters; the eyewitness account of the Rethel meeting of 17 August and of the 5th Army's retreat. Partisan towards the BEF; check against the official histories.

author: Ludendorff, Erich
title: My War Memories, 1914–1918 (Meine Kriegserinnerungen 1914–1918)
publisher: Hutchinson, London; E. S. Mittler, Berlin
notes: Ludendorff's memoir; the first-hand account of the 14th Brigade's night march into Liège and the surrender of the citadel on 7 August 1914. Self-serving on everything after; reliable for the Liège episode where the Reichsarchiv agrees.

author: Foch, Ferdinand
title: Mémoires pour servir à l'histoire de la guerre de 1914–1918
notes: Foch's memoirs; for the 9th Army at the marshes of Saint-Gond, 6–10 September 1914 — notably silent on the 'situation excellente, j'attaque' line attributed to him.

author: Gallieni, Joseph
title: Mémoires du général Gallieni: Défense de Paris, 25 août – 11 septembre 1914
notes: Gallieni's own account (he died in 1916; published by his family), with a documents annex printing the Paris orders of 3–9 September (Ordre général no 5 of 4 September, the proclamation of 3 September). Written to assert Gallieni's priority over Joffre in the Marne decision; cite the documents, treat the narrative as one side of that dispute. Also the account of the Paris camp and the 6th Army's attack on the Ourcq, including the requisition of the Paris taxis on 6–7 September 1914.

author: Kluck, Alexander von
title: The March on Paris and the Battle of the Marne, 1914
edition: English translation of Der Marsch auf Paris und die Marneschlacht 1914 (Mittler, Berlin, 1920), with notes by the Historical Section (Military Branch) of the Committee of Imperial Defence
notes: First Army commander's memoir, completed February 1918. Prints the OHL directives of 27 August and 4 September, the Bülow–Kluck wireless exchange of 30–31 August and the First Army minute of Hentsch's instructions of 9 September. Self-justifying on the turn inside Paris and on Hentsch; cite for what Kluck's headquarters received and believed, not as fact.

author: Ministère de la Guerre, État-major de l'Armée, Service historique
title: Les Armées françaises dans la Grande Guerre, Tome I, 2e volume: Annexes, 1er volume
notes: The order annexes for 24 August – 5 September 1914: Instruction générale no 2 (annexe no 395, 25 August), Joffre's telegrams and the army orders of the retreat. Authoritative for the French texts; page references are to the printed volume (Gallica scan page = printed page + 14).

author: Ministère des Affaires étrangères de Belgique
title: Correspondance diplomatique relative à la guerre de 1914 (24 juillet – 29 août): the Belgian Grey Book
publisher: Brussels; English translation in Collected Diplomatic Documents relating to the Outbreak of the European War (HMSO, London, 1915)
notes: The Belgian government's published diplomatic file: No. 20 the German note of 2 August (German text and translation), No. 22 the Belgian reply of 3 August, No. 71 the memorandum on the delivery. A belligerent's publication, selected for effect on neutral opinion; the texts themselves are authentic. The BYU transcription carries OCR slips, corrected silently.

author: Le Radical (Paris)
title: Le Radical, 5 août 1914 — 'La réponse de la Belgique', p. 2
notes: Paris daily printing the French text of the Belgian reply as released on 4 August; used for the French wording (checked against Le Rappel and La Gazette de France of the same date, and Poincaré, Comment fut déclarée la guerre de 1914, 1939). Newspaper OCR; a few typographic slips corrected by comparison.

author: Bayerische Staatsbibliothek (ed.); Epkenhans, Michael (introduction)
title: Alfred Graf von Schlieffen, Denkschrift 'Krieg gegen Frankreich' [Schlieffen-Plan], Dezember 1905 — Volltext und Faksimile
notes: Full German transcription (with Moltke's marginalia) and facsimile of the Boetticher copy, Bundesarchiv-Militärarchiv N 323/19, with an introduction by Epkenhans summarising the Zuber debate. The text quoted in the Document card.

author: Ehlert, Hans; Epkenhans, Michael; Groß, Gerhard P. (eds)
title: Der Schlieffenplan: Analysen und Dokumente
notes: The post-Zuber collection: essays (Groß, 'There was a Schlieffen Plan') and the edited documents, including the December 1905 memorandum and the later Aufmarschanweisungen. For the historiography panel and the German text.

author: Ritter, Gerhard
title: The Schlieffen Plan: Critique of a Myth
edition: translation of Der Schlieffenplan: Kritik eines Mythos (Munich, 1956)
notes: First publication of the 1905 memorandum and its drafts, with Moltke's comments, from the then-lost-and-recovered files; the English text of the memorandum is at pp. 134–148. Ritter's critique of the plan's feasibility is itself a position in the debate.

author: Van Pul, Paul
title: In Flanders Flooded Fields: Before Ypres There Was Yser
notes: Specialist study of the Yser inundation by a hydraulic engineer: the polder system, the locks of the Ganzepoot at Nieuwpoort, and who opened which sluice on which night. Reconstructs the operation of 21–30 October 1914 from the Belgian engineering and unit records, and argues against the older claim that Foch was the author of the idea; the flooding is his subject, the wider battle only its frame.

author: Unruh, Karl
title: Langemarck: Legende und Wirklichkeit
notes: The detailed demolition of the Langemarck legend: the composition of the four new reserve corps (experienced reservists and Landwehr with a minority of volunteers, not a student army), the absence of the singing from contemporary accounts, and the distance between the fighting of late October and the communiqué of 11 November. Cite for the reality against which the myth is measured.

author: Grawe, Lukas
title: Langemarck Myth
publisher: 1914-1918-online. International Encyclopedia of the First World War (Freie Universität Berlin)
notes: Peer-reviewed encyclopedia article: the text of the OHL communiqué of 11 November 1914, the fighting it actually described (10 November, between Bixschote and Noordschote), the composition of the reserve corps, and the myth's later career. Cite for the communiqué's wording and the myth's construction.

author: Jones, Spencer
title: Ypres, Battles of
publisher: 1914-1918-online. International Encyclopedia of the First World War (Freie Universität Berlin)
notes: Peer-reviewed encyclopedia article on the Ypres battles; for First Ypres gives 19 October – 22 November 1914, the armies engaged, German losses of about 130,000 and Entente losses of about 100,000, and the destruction of the British pre-war army. Cite for the round totals beside Edmonds's exact returns.

author: Clark, Christopher
title: The Sleepwalkers: How Europe Went to War in 1914
notes: The leading revisionist account of the July Crisis: decision-makers as sleepwalkers rather than conspirators, with Serbian and Balkan agency given full weight and German war guilt distributed across all the chancelleries. Cite as one position in the origins debate, against Fischer.

author: Fischer, Fritz
title: Germany's Aims in the First World War
edition: translation of Griff nach der Weltmacht (Dusseldorf, 1961)
notes: The book that broke the post-1918 consensus: Germany deliberately courted a continental war in July 1914 in pursuit of world power. The thesis every later account of the crisis argues with; cite as a position, not as settled fact.

author: Albertini, Luigi
title: The Origins of the War of 1914
edition: 3 vols, translated by Isabella M. Massey, 1952-1957
notes: The most detailed narrative reconstruction of the crisis, hour by hour, built on the diplomatic documents and on interviews with surviving participants. Still the standard reference for what was sent, received and understood on each day.

author: Mombauer, Annika
title: The Origins of the First World War: Diplomatic and Military Documents
notes: Scholarly edition of the crisis documents in English translation with commentary, drawn from the national colour books and the post-war editions; useful for checking a text against the archival original and for the editorial history of the collections.

author: Great Britain, Foreign Office
title: Collected Diplomatic Documents Relating to the Outbreak of the European War
notes: The belligerents' own published files - the British Blue Book, the German White Book, the Austro-Hungarian Red Book, the Serbian Blue Book, the Russian Orange Book, the Belgian Grey Book - gathered in one English volume. Each colour book was selected and, in places, edited by its government for effect on neutral opinion; the texts are authentic but the selection is not neutral.

author: Kautsky, Karl; Montgelas, Max; Schucking, Walther
title: Outbreak of the World War: German Documents Collected by Karl Kautsky
edition: English translation of Die Deutschen Dokumente zum Kriegsausbruch (Berlin, 1919)
notes: The German foreign-office files on the crisis, published by the new republic to document the old regime's conduct; the collection in which the 'blank cheque' telegram of 6 July 1914 is document no. 15. Compiled with a political purpose - to show the Kaiser's government at fault - but the texts are the archival ones.

author: Brigham Young University Library
title: The World War I Document Archive
notes: Transcriptions of the published diplomatic collections. Used here for the working text of documents whose authoritative printing is cited alongside it; the transcriptions carry occasional OCR slips, corrected silently against the printed collection.

author: Doughty, Robert A.
title: Pyrrhic Victory: French Strategy and Operations in the Great War
publisher: Belknap Press of Harvard University Press, Cambridge MA
notes: The standard operational history of the French army in the war, written from the AFGG and the GQG archives; the spine for Plan XVII, the Ardennes offensive and Joffre's handling of his army commanders.

author: Greenhalgh, Elizabeth
title: The French Army and the First World War
notes: Armies of the Great War series; cited here for the Colonial Corps' losses at Rossignol on 22 August 1914 (p. 41) and for the state of French doctrine in August.

author: Zuber, Terence
title: The Battle of the Frontiers: Ardennes 1914
notes: The only monograph on the Ardennes encounter battles, built from German regimental histories. Zuber's wider argument about the 'Schlieffen Plan' is contested (see source:zuber-2002 and source:mombauer-2001); his tactical reconstruction of 21–23 August is used here for the shape of the fighting, not for its conclusions.

author: Foley, Robert T. (ed. and trans.)
title: Alfred von Schlieffen's Military Writings
notes: Schlieffen's staff rides, war games and memoranda in translation, with Foley's introduction. Cited for what Schlieffen actually wrote as against what the post-war General Staff said he had planned; one of the principal replies to Zuber.

author: Holmes, Terence M.
title: The Reluctant March on Paris: A Reply to Terence Zuber's 'The Schlieffen Plan Reconsidered'
notes: The opening reply in the War in History exchange that ran from 1999 into the 2010s. Cited for the case that the December 1905 memorandum describes a real operational intention; Zuber's rejoinders are part of the same exchange and the pack presents both sides.

author: Showalter, Dennis E.
title: Tannenberg: Clash of Empires, 1914
edition: first published Archon Books, Hamden CT, 1991
notes: The standard operational account of the East Prussian campaign of August 1914: Gumbinnen, the relief of Prittwitz, the encirclement, and the two corps sent from the West.

author: Stone, Norman
title: The Eastern Front 1914-1917
notes: The Eastern Front as a whole, sceptical of the Tannenberg legend and of the German high command's later account of it; cite for the campaign's shape and for the myth-making.

author: Sumpf, Alban
title: Les taxis de la Marne
publisher: L'Histoire par l'image (Réunion des musées nationaux – Grand Palais; with the French ministries of Culture and of National Education)
notes: A short curated study written around the period photographs of the requisition. Cited for the lower end of the taxi arithmetic — 630 taxis and more than 3,000 men of the 103rd and 104th Infantry, requisitioned by Gallieni on 6 September 1914 — and for the judgement that the trains carried the overwhelming majority of the reinforcements and the taxis were not decisive. It is a public-history site rather than an archival study: use it for the figures it states and for the episode's memory, not for the operational narrative, which comes from the AFGG and Herwig.

author: Bruce, Robert B.
title: Pétain: Verdun to Vichy
notes: A short scholarly biography in the Potomac Military Profiles series. Cited here for the organisation of motor supply at Verdun in 1916 — the Bar-le-Duc–Verdun road divided into six sections with repair shops, refuelling points, a commanding officer and traffic police; the Service automobile and the Bar-le-Duc traffic commission at some 9,000 officers and men with 3,900 vehicles; and the first fortnight's loads of 190,000 men, 22,500 tons of munitions and 2,500 tons of other materiel. Sympathetic to Pétain as a commander, which is the bias to watch on the Verdun chapters; the figures are the ones the French service histories give.

author: Mémorial de Verdun
title: La bataille de Verdun (museum resource page)
publisher: Mémorial de Verdun – Champ de bataille, Fleury-devant-Douaumont
notes: The battlefield museum's own account. Cited only for the traffic figures it states for the Bar-le-Duc–Verdun road: 3,500 lorries, 2,000 cars and 800 ambulances in rotation, a lorry every 14 seconds and one vehicle every 5 seconds at the June–July peak, 90,000 men and 50,000 tonnes a week, and 1,200 territorials shovelling 700,000 tonnes of stone. These are the round figures French commemoration has settled on rather than archival returns, and the card says so; the specific loads come from Bruce.

author: Einstein, Albert
title: Zur Elektrodynamik bewegter Körper
publisher: Annalen der Physik 322 (ser. 4, vol. 17), no. 10, pp. 891–921
notes: The special-relativity paper: received 30 June 1905, published 26 September 1905. Cite for what the paper contains and for its date; contemporary volume numbering is 17, the modern continuous series numbering is 322.

author: Einstein, Albert
title: Ist die Trägheit eines Körpers von seinem Energieinhalt abhängig?
publisher: Annalen der Physik 323 (ser. 4, vol. 18), no. 13, pp. 639–641
notes: Three pages; the mass–energy relation, written as a body radiating energy L losing mass L/c². Cite for what the paper says, not for anything later done with it.

author: Bohr, Niels
title: On the Constitution of Atoms and Molecules, Parts I–III
publisher: Philosophical Magazine, ser. 6, vol. 26: pp. 1–25 (no. 151, July), 476–502 (no. 153, September), 857–875 (no. 155, November)
notes: The quantum atom as Bohr first stated it. Cite for the model, the stationary states and the hydrogen spectrum; the three parts are one argument and are cited here as one work.

author: Moseley, Henry G. J.
title: The High-Frequency Spectra of the Elements, Parts I and II
publisher: Philosophical Magazine, ser. 6, vol. 26, pp. 1024–1034 (December 1913); vol. 27, pp. 703–713 (April 1914)
notes: Moseley's law and the atomic number, in the two papers that established it. Part II is the one that fixes the gaps at 43, 61, 72 and 75. Cite for the physics and for the papers' dates.

author: Einstein, Albert
title: Erklärung der Perihelbewegung des Merkur aus der allgemeinen Relativitätstheorie
publisher: Sitzungsberichte der Königlich Preußischen Akademie der Wissenschaften (Berlin), 1915, pp. 831–839
notes: Read 18 November 1915: Mercury's anomalous perihelion advance and the doubled light deflection, on field equations Einstein revised again a week later. Cite for the perihelion result and the date.

author: Einstein, Albert
title: Die Feldgleichungen der Gravitation
publisher: Sitzungsberichte der Königlich Preußischen Akademie der Wissenschaften (Berlin), 1915, pp. 844–847
notes: Read 25 November 1915; four pages, the last of the four November papers, and the field equations in their final form. Cite for the equations and the date, not for the priority argument with Hilbert.

author: Corry, Leo; Renn, Jürgen; Stachel, John
title: Belated Decision in the Hilbert-Einstein Priority Dispute
notes: The printer's proofs of Hilbert's paper of 20 November 1915, read as showing that what Hilbert first submitted was not generally covariant and did not contain the explicit field equations. One side of a live argument — Winterberg (2004) and others dispute the reading of the proofs; cite it as a position, not a verdict.

author: Schwarzschild, Karl
title: Über das Gravitationsfeld eines Massenpunktes nach der Einsteinschen Theorie
publisher: Sitzungsberichte der Königlich Preußischen Akademie der Wissenschaften (Berlin), 1916, pp. 189–196
notes: The first exact solution of the field equations, written on the Russian front and presented for the author by Einstein on 13 January 1916. The header carries the presentation date; the paper opens by naming the problem Einstein set in the Mercury paper of 18 November 1915.

author: Schulmann, Robert; Kox, A. J.; Janssen, Michel; Illy, József (eds)
title: The Collected Papers of Albert Einstein, Volume 8: The Berlin Years — Correspondence, 1914–1918
notes: The wartime correspondence. Schwarzschild's letter of 22 December 1915 enclosing his solution is doc. 169; quotations here follow the English supplement translation and are cited as translations.

author: Voigt, Hans-Heinrich (ed.)
title: Karl Schwarzschild: Gesammelte Werke / Collected Works, Volume 1
notes: The collected works, opening with the biographical essay: Schwarzschild's war service (weather station in Belgium, artillery trajectory work in France, then Russia), the pemphigus contracted at the front, the return home in March 1916 and his death on 11 May 1916.

author: Noether, Emmy
title: Invariante Variationsprobleme
publisher: Nachrichten von der Königlichen Gesellschaft der Wissenschaften zu Göttingen, Mathematisch-Physikalische Klasse, 1918, pp. 235–257
notes: The two Noether theorems. Presented for her by Felix Klein at the session of 26 July 1918, Noether not being a member; dedicated to Klein. Cite for the theorems and the date.

author: Kosmann-Schwarzbach, Yvette
title: The Noether Theorems: Invariance and Conservation Laws in the Twentieth Century
notes: Translation of the 1918 paper with a scholarly history of both theorems and their reception, including the energy-conservation problem in general relativity that Hilbert and Klein set her. The standard modern treatment.

author: Dick, Auguste
title: Emmy Noether 1882–1935
notes: The standard short biography (translated from the 1970 German). Cite for the Göttingen years: the refused habilitation, the courses announced under Hilbert's name, the habilitation of 1919 and the unsalaried years to 1923.

author: Rutherford, Ernest
title: Collision of α Particles with Light Atoms, Parts I–IV
publisher: Philosophical Magazine, ser. 6, vol. 37, no. 222, pp. 537–587; Part IV, 'An anomalous effect in nitrogen', pp. 581–587
notes: The four papers reporting the first artificial disintegration of a nucleus. Cite for what Rutherford observed and concluded in 1919 — not for the reaction as now written, which is Blackett (1925).

author: Blackett, Patrick M. S.
title: The Ejection of Protons from Nitrogen Nuclei, Photographed by the Wilson Method
publisher: Proceedings of the Royal Society A 107, pp. 349–360
notes: The cloud-chamber photographs — eight forked tracks in some 400,000 — showing that the alpha particle is absorbed and not scattered, so that the 1919 result is a transmutation of nitrogen into oxygen. Cite for the corrected reading of Rutherford's experiment.

author: Eve, Arthur Stewart
title: Rutherford: Being the Life and Letters of the Rt Hon. Lord Rutherford, O.M.
notes: The letters-and-recollections life by a colleague; the source for most of the well-known Rutherford anecdotes, including the reply about the missed anti-submarine meetings and the 'moonshine' remark of 1933. Cite the anecdotes as anecdotes — Eve rarely dates or stages them precisely, and later tellings vary.

author: Wilson, David
title: Rutherford: Simple Genius
notes: The modern biography. Cite for the wartime work on submarine detection for the Admiralty's Board of Invention and Research, the Manchester nitrogen experiments alongside it, and the move to the Cavendish in 1919.

author: Pais, Abraham
title: Niels Bohr's Times: In Physics, Philosophy, and Polity
notes: The companion volume to Pais's Einstein biography: Bohr's Manchester year, the 1913 trilogy and its reception, and Bohr's later life. Same strength and same bias as Pais on Einstein — a physicist writing about physics, thin on the social setting.

author: Dyson, Frank W.; Eddington, Arthur S.; Davidson, Charles
title: A Determination of the Deflection of Light by the Sun's Gravitational Field, from Observations Made at the Total Eclipse of May 29, 1919
publisher: Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society A 220, pp. 291–333
notes: The expedition report itself: the three plate sets, the reductions, the published deflections and the stated grounds for setting the Sobral astrographic plates aside. Cite for the numbers as published; the argument about whether the rejection was justified is Earman & Glymour, Kennefick and Gilmore & Tausch-Pebody.

author: Earman, John; Glymour, Clark
title: Relativity and Eclipses: The British Eclipse Expeditions of 1919 and Their Predecessors
publisher: Historical Studies in the Physical Sciences 11, no. 1, pp. 49–85
notes: The case that the 1919 announcement outran its data and that the discordant plates were dropped because they disagreed with Einstein. The sceptical side of the argument; cite it as one side.

author: Kennefick, Daniel
title: No Shadow of a Doubt: The 1919 Eclipse That Confirmed Einstein's Theory of Relativity
notes: The reply to Earman & Glymour, developed from Kennefick's 2009 Physics Today article: the astrographic plates were rejected by Dyson on instrumental grounds, and Dyson, not Eddington, made the call. The defending side; cite it as one side.

author: Gilmore, Gerard; Tausch-Pebody, Gudrun
title: The 1919 Eclipse Results That Verified General Relativity and Their Later Detractors: A Story Re-told
publisher: Notes and Records of the Royal Society 76, no. 1, pp. 155–180
notes: A re-examination of the 1919 reductions and of the twentieth-century criticism of them, concluding that the published result stands. The most recent round of the argument; cite alongside Earman & Glymour, not instead of them.

author: Museum of the History of Science, University of Oxford
title: 'Dear Harry…' — Henry Moseley: A Scientist Lost to War
notes: The museum's exhibition and research site, built on Moseley's letters and the family papers it holds. Cite for the circumstances of his death on 10 August 1915 — the 38th Brigade signal section, the Turkish counter-attack on Chunuk Bair, the body never recovered, the name on the Helles Memorial — and for the 1915 Nobel nominations.

author: Haber, L. F.
title: The Poisonous Cloud: Chemical Warfare in the First World War
notes: The standard scholarly account of chemical warfare in the war, and the source everyone else's casualty table comes from: p. 243 gives about 186,000 gas casualties for Britain, 130,000 for France, 107,000 for Germany and 73,000 for the United States. Its verdict is that gas was militarily disappointing and a poor return on the industry it consumed. Ludwig Fritz Haber was Fritz Haber's son and an economic historian; he says so, and the book is markedly unsentimental about his father — the bias to watch is a professional economist's scepticism about the weapon's value, not filial defence.

author: Faith, Thomas I.
title: Gas Warfare
publisher: 1914-1918-online. International Encyclopedia of the First World War (Freie Universität Berlin)
notes: Peer-reviewed survey article. Cited for the sequence of first uses — French tear-gas rifle grenades in August 1914, German irritant shell at Neuve-Chapelle in October 1914 and at Bolimów in January 1915, all ineffective; chlorine at Ypres on 22 April 1915 under Haber's direction; phosgene in December 1915; mustard in July 1917 — and for the four-nation casualty table it reprints from Haber (1986) with the caveat that gas casualty data are inherently inaccurate and that for some nations only generalized estimates exist.

author: Heller, Charles E.
title: Chemical Warfare in World War I: The American Experience, 1917–1918
publisher: Combat Studies Institute, US Army Command and General Staff College, Fort Leavenworth (Leavenworth Papers No. 10)
notes: A staff-college study, open access, with a careful narrative of the first gas attacks before it reaches the American chapters. Cited for the mechanics of 22 April 1915 — the release in the early evening, the two French divisions hit (the 87th Territorial and the 45th Algerian) and the gap of about four miles — and for the first French phosgene shells at Verdun on 22 February 1916. It is a doctrinal study written to draw lessons for the US Army, so its interest is in what worked and why; the operational judgements are conventional.

author: Fitzgerald, Gerard J.
title: Chemical Warfare and Medical Response During World War I
notes: Peer-reviewed and open access; the medical and public-health side of gas warfare. Cited for the high end of the casualty range — more than 1.3 million gas casualties and approximately 90,000 deaths by the armistice — and for the ratio inside it: of about 186,000 British chemical casualties, a death toll of about 2.6 per cent, and of the AEF's gas casualties about 1,500 died. Its judgement is that chemical weapons killed proportionally few soldiers and that a chlorine or phosgene attack produced many casualties but few deaths against troops properly prepared and outfitted. Written from the medical literature rather than the operational archives, and one sentence in it garbles the share of casualties gas caused — take the figures it attributes, not its arithmetic.

author: Kramer, Alan
title: Naval Blockade (of Germany)
publisher: 1914-1918-online. International Encyclopedia of the First World War (Freie Universität Berlin)
notes: Peer-reviewed survey of the blockade and its effects. Cited for the nitrogen figures: BASF producing the annual equivalent of 6,000 tons of nitrogen as ammonium sulphate by July 1914, output raised to 200,000 tons a year under a state guarantee, and German industry supplying 90 per cent of the nitrogen for explosives and 70 per cent of agricultural demand by the end of 1915. Kramer's argument elsewhere in the article is that the blockade's effects on German civilians were severe and are understated in some of the literature — a position to note, though the nitrogen figures are not the contested part.

author: Friedrich, Bretislav; Hoffmann, Dieter
title: Clara Haber, née Immerwahr (1870–1915): Life, Work and Legacy
publisher: Zeitschrift für anorganische und allgemeine Chemie 642(6), 437–448
notes: The scholarly reassessment of Clara Immerwahr, by a Fritz Haber Institute director and a historian of science, published with a companion piece by Eckart Henning ('Freitod in Dahlem (1915)', same issue, 432–436). Cited for the doctorate at Breslau in 1900 and for the historiography of her death: that neither Clara nor Fritz Haber left diaries or correspondence from which her motives could be reconstructed, that no farewell letter survives, and that the reading of her suicide as a protest against chemical weapons rests on later authors — Morris Goran in 1947 and 1967, and Gerit von Leitner's Der Fall Clara Immerwahr (1993) — who give no sources for it. Friedrich and Hoffmann are correcting a myth and press their case hard; the pack states their position as a position and names the popular reading beside it.

author: Erisman, Jan Willem; Sutton, Mark A.; Galloway, James; Klimont, Zbigniew; Winiwarter, Wilfried
title: How a century of ammonia synthesis changed the world
notes: The centenary assessment of the Haber–Bosch process, by nitrogen-cycle scientists rather than historians. Cited for the patent date — Haber filed on 13 October 1908 on the 'synthesis of ammonia from its elements' — and for its own summary that a hundred years on 'we live in a world transformed by and highly dependent upon Haber–Bosch nitrogen'. The paper's often-quoted estimate of the share of world population fed by synthetic nitrogen is behind the paywall and is deliberately not quoted here.

author: The Nobel Foundation
title: The Nobel Prize in Chemistry 1918 — Fritz Haber
notes: The awarding body's own record. Cited only for the prize itself: the Chemistry prize for 1918 to Fritz Haber 'for the synthesis of ammonia from its elements', reserved and awarded in 1919, with the Nobel lecture delivered in June 1920. Reference data, in the same register as the biographical dates rule in docs/sources.md — not a source for anything about the gas programme.

author: Reichsarchiv
title: Der Weltkrieg 1914 bis 1918. Die militärischen Operationen zu Lande, Band 3: Der Marne-Feldzug — Von der Sambre zur Marne
notes: German official history, the volume between the frontier battles and the Marne: the operations of the German western armies from the Sambre to the Marne, roughly 23 August to 4 September 1914. It names, day by day and in its own words, the town each Armee-Oberkommando moved its Hauptquartier to, which is this pack's citation for the German commander tracks over the advance; it also carries the move of the Große Hauptquartier from Koblenz to Luxembourg on the morning of 30 August (p. 190). Bd. 4, which would carry the battle itself and Moltke's tour of 11 September, is not digitised. Apologetic on command decisions, like Bd. 1, and it measures the campaign by what the German army did.

author: Edmonds, J. E.
title: Military Operations: France and Belgium, 1914, Volume I: Mons, the Retreat to the Seine, the Marne and the Aisne, August–October 1914
publisher: Macmillan, London (History of the Great War based on Official Documents)
edition: Third edition, 1933 (reprinted 1937) — a thorough revision of the 1922 first edition against the French and German official histories; its pagination differs from the first edition's
notes: The edition of Edmonds Vol. I that is digitised and was read, and therefore the one this pack cites whenever it gives a page number for the BEF in 1914. It names where GHQ was on most nights of the retreat and prints the GHQ operation orders in its appendices, which is this pack's citation for the GHQ track. Do not carry page numbers between this and source:edmonds-1922.

author: Lanrezac, Charles
title: Le plan de campagne français et le premier mois de la guerre (2 août – 3 septembre 1914)
notes: The French 5th Army commander's own book, published after his relief and written to answer it. Day by day, and it names his own headquarters — Rethel, Chimay, the command post at Philippeville on the day of Charleroi, Sézanne — which is this pack's citation for the 5th Army track. It also gives the hour Joffre reached Sézanne on 3 September to relieve him (p. 276). Self-exculpatory throughout on the retreat from Charleroi and on the BEF; cite for where his headquarters was and what he says he was told, and check the judgements against the official histories.
